items.title: Aggressive driving: what it is
items.simple: An aggressive driver breaks traffic laws on purpose to scare, bother, hurt or block others. They tailgate, weave, speed, run red lights and pass on the shoulder.
items.official: Defined by Virginia law as the intent to harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct another person while committing one or more traffic offenses such as failing to stop or yield the right-of-way, avoiding a traffic control device or failing to give way to an overtaking vehicle. Aggressive drivers run stop signs and red lights, speed, tailgate, weave in and out of traffic, pass on the right (including on the shoulder and unpaved portions of the road), make improper and unsafe lane changes, make hand and facial gestures, scream, honk and flash their lights.

items.title: Stay away from aggressive drivers
items.simple: If you see an aggressive driver, stay out of the way. Do not speed up or race them. Do not look them in the eye. Ignore their yelling and hand signs.
items.official: Protect yourself. If you see an aggressive driver, stay out of the way. Don't challenge the aggressive driver by speeding up or trying to out-maneuver him. Avoid eye contact and ignore his gestures and shouting.
items.mnemonic: Don't race, don't face. Let them pass.

items.title: Aggressive driving: 10 days-6 months
items.simple: If you are convicted (found guilty) of aggressive driving, you can lose your license. The suspension can last 10 days or as long as 6 months.
items.official: If you are convicted of aggressive driving, your license could be suspended for ten days or for as long as six months.
items.mnemonic: Road rage costs 10 days up to half a year (6 months).

items.title: Many things can distract you
items.simple: Driving needs all of your attention. Many things can distract you, such as changing the music or GPS, talking to passengers, eating, using a phone and looking at sights outside.
items.official: Driving requires your full attention. There are many distractions that may prevent drivers from focusing on driving: changing the music selection/podcast/GPS, talking to passengers, observing outside surroundings, eating, using a cell phone and more.

items.title: No holding a phone
items.simple: In Virginia, you may not hold a phone while you drive. There are two exceptions. One is a driver emergency. The other is when your car is legally parked or stopped.
items.official: Virginia law prohibits drivers from holding cell phones or any other wireless communication devices while driving except in a driver emergency or the vehicle is lawfully parked or stopped.
items.mnemonic: Hands on the wheel, phone out of hand.

items.title: Phone GPS: no holding or typing
items.simple: You may use a phone for directions (GPS) while you drive. But you may not hold it or type into it. Set it up before you go.
items.official: A mobile phone or other telecommunications device may be used for navigation, as long as the driver is not entering information or holding it while driving.
items.mnemonic: GPS: set it, then forget it.

items.title: Distraction: 17% of crashes
items.simple: Distraction causes about 17 percent of all crashes in Virginia each year. While you look away, your car can drift into danger. You lose seconds that you need in order to react.
items.official: Annually, driver distraction accounts for roughly 17 percent of all traffic crashes in Virginia. While the driver is distracted, the vehicle may move into a high risk situation. The driver then loses precious seconds before recognizing the situation and must make an emergency maneuver. Young distracted drivers are even more susceptible. Failure to maintain proper control, following too closely, and not yielding the right-of-way are common actions of young distracted drivers.

items.title: Eyes on road, hands on wheel
items.simple: Keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the wheel. Set up controls and devices before you drive. Do not use a phone. To do something distracting, pull over and stop first.
items.official: Drivers should not use cell phones, computers or other distracting devices except to report a crash or emergency. Before engaging in distracting behavior, pull over and stop the vehicle in a safe location. Keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the wheel at all times. Set or adjust the controls on the vehicle and other devices as soon as you get in the car and before you begin driving. Do not use a cell phone.

items.title: Signs you are too sleepy
items.simple: Watch for signs that you are too sleepy. You yawn a lot, nod your head or have heavy eyelids. You cannot remember the last few miles. You miss exits, drift into other lanes or hit rumble strips.
items.official: Constant yawning, head nodding, heavy eyelids, difficulty remembering the last few miles driven, missing road signs or exits, unplanned lane changes, driving off the road or hitting rumble strips are all signs of drowsy driving. Driving while you are sleepy increases your crash risk as you struggle to process complex information coming from different places at once. You may make careless driving decisions, have trouble paying attention or actually fall asleep while driving. Drowsy driving is a type of impaired driving.
items.mnemonic: Yawn, nod, drift? Time to stop.

items.title: Prevent drowsy driving
items.simple: Before a trip, get plenty of good sleep. Skip alcohol and heavy foods. Watch out for medicines that affect driving. If you can, bring a friend and switch drivers. Always let a well-rested person drive.
items.official: To avoid drowsy driving: get plenty of quality sleep before a trip; avoid alcoholic beverages and heavy foods; beware of medications that can impair your driving ability; if possible, drive with a companion and switch drivers when necessary. Always let a well-rested person drive.

items.title: Rest every two hours
items.simple: Limit long drives. On a long trip, stop to rest at least every two hours.
items.official: Limit long distance driving. Stop at least every two hours for rest.
items.mnemonic: Two hours, take a rest.

items.title: A 10-20 minute nap helps
items.simple: If you are sleepy, stop at a safe place and take a nap. Just 10 to 20 minutes of sleep can make a big difference.
items.official: Stop at a safe place and take a nap. As little as 10 to 20 minutes of sleep can make a big difference.
items.mnemonic: Sleepy? Stop and nap 10 to 20 minutes.

items.title: Avoid driving 10 p.m.-6 a.m.
items.simple: To avoid drowsy driving, try not to drive between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
items.official: To avoid drowsy driving: Avoid driving from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.
items.mnemonic: 10 to 6: sleep, don't drive.

items.title: Coffee and radio don't fix sleepy
items.simple: Rolling down a window, chewing gum, turning up the radio, and drinking coffee or energy drinks do NOT stop drowsy driving. You cannot count on them to keep you awake. Stop and rest instead.
items.official: Rolling down a window, chewing gum, turning up the radio, or consuming caffeine, energy drinks or other stimulants do not prevent drowsy driving and are not reliable methods for staying awake.
items.mnemonic: Gum, radio, window, coffee: no. Rest: yes.

items.title: See a drowsy driver? Report it
items.simple: If you see a drowsy driver, find a safe place to stop or ask a passenger to call the police. Be ready to describe the location, the car and what the driver did.
items.official: If you observe a drowsy driver, find a safe place to stop or ask a passenger to call law enforcement. Be able to describe the location, vehicle and actions you observed.
items.mnemonic: Tell police 3 things: where, what car, what it did.

items.title: Age 21+: DUI at .08 BAC
items.simple: BAC means blood alcohol content. If you are 21 or older, a BAC of .08 or higher is DUI. DUI means driving under the influence.
items.official: Legally, drivers age 21 or older are considered to be driving under the influence (DUI) if your blood alcohol content (BAC) is .08 percent or higher.
items.mnemonic: 21 and over: .08 is a DUI.

items.title: Under .08 can still be DUI
items.simple: Even if your BAC is under .08, you can still get a DUI. If alcohol impairs your driving, that is enough.
items.official: If your driving is impaired, you can be convicted of driving under the influence with a BAC lower than .08 percent.
items.mnemonic: Under .08 is not a free pass.

items.title: Under 21: .02 BAC is illegal
items.simple: If you are under 21, a BAC from .02 to just under .08 counts as illegal drinking. With a BAC of .08 or higher, you could get a DUI.
items.official: If under age 21, you can be convicted of illegal consumption of alcohol if your BAC is at least .02 but less than .08. If your BAC is .08 or higher you could be convicted of a DUI.
items.mnemonic: Under 21: .02 and you're through.

items.title: Late night: 3 in 10 drunk
items.simple: Between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m., about 3 out of every 10 drivers are drunk. More than 1 in 3 of them drank at someone else's home. In your lifetime, you have a 50-50 chance of an alcohol-related crash.
items.official: Researchers estimate that between the hours of 10 PM and 2 AM three out of every ten drivers are drunk. More than one-third of these drivers have been drinking at someone else's home. Nearly 50 percent of the drivers arrested for DUI are social to moderate drinkers. In your lifetime, there's a 50-50 chance that you'll be involved in an alcohol-related crash.
items.mnemonic: 10 to 2: 3 in 10 are drunk.

items.title: One drink changes your driving
items.simple: Just one drink can hurt your driving. Even a little alcohol affects your brain. It harms your vision, your judgment and your coordination.
items.official: Just one alcoholic drink can affect your driving ability because even a small amount of alcohol affects the brain's functions - particularly vision, judgment, and coordination.
items.mnemonic: One drink hurts how you See, Think and Move (vision, judgment, coordination).

items.title: Drinking: 7 times crash risk
items.simple: Driving after drinking makes a crash 7 times more likely than driving sober.
items.official: Because alcohol affects your judgment and driving ability, your chances of being in a crash are seven times greater if you drive after drinking than if you drive sober.
items.mnemonic: Drink and drive: 7 times the risk.

items.title: Beer, shot, wine: same alcohol
items.simple: One 12-ounce beer is the same as one shot of liquor. It is also the same as one 5-ounce glass of wine. A beer counts as much as a shot.
items.official: Twelve ounces of beer is the same as a shot of liquor or a five-ounce glass of wine.
items.mnemonic: 12-5-1: a 12-ounce beer = a 5-ounce wine = 1 shot.

items.title: Only time sobers you up
items.simple: Only time can sober you up. Coffee, cold showers and exercise will not sober you up.
items.official: Only time can decrease intoxication. Coffee, cold showers or exercise will not sober you up.
items.mnemonic: No shortcut: only time.

items.title: Decide before you drink
items.simple: Alcohol-related crashes are not accidents. They can be prevented. Decide before you drink that you will not drive. Plan a sober ride home. Deciding not to drive gets harder after one or two drinks.
items.official: Alcohol-related crashes are not accidents. They can be prevented! The only way to avoid the risks of drinking and driving is to decide before you start drinking that you are not going to drive. Making the decision not to drive is a lot more difficult after one or two drinks. When attending a social event where alcohol will be consumed, plan ahead for a sober ride home by using alternative transportation or having a sober driver.
items.mnemonic: Plan the ride before the drink.

items.title: Alcohol plus drugs multiplies
items.simple: Mixing alcohol with other drugs usually multiplies the effects of both. One drink taken with another drug can affect you as much as several drinks. Even aspirin or cold medicine counts as a drug.
items.official: Combining alcohol with other drugs usually multiplies the effects of both and can have a disastrous effect on your ability to drive. One drink taken when you are on another drug - even an aspirin, or allergy or cold medicine - could have the same effect on your driving ability as drinking several alcoholic beverages.
items.mnemonic: Mix means multiply.

items.title: Medicine can affect driving
items.simple: Many store-bought and prescription medicines can make you sleepy or dizzy. This includes pills, syrups, drops and sprays. Read the label. If you are not sure, ask a pharmacist or doctor.
items.official: Almost any drug can reduce your ability to drive safely. It's not just illegal drugs that cause problems. Many over-the-counter medications and prescription drugs for headaches, hay fever, colds, allergies or nervous conditions can cause drowsiness and dizziness. This includes syrups, drops, sprays, pills and tablets. They often affect driver alertness and slow reaction time. Read the label before taking any drug or medicine. Look for warnings about side effects. If you're uncertain about the effects of a drug, ask your pharmacist or doctor. No drug is harmless.
items.mnemonic: No drug is harmless. Read the label first.

items.title: Drugged driving is DUI too
items.simple: Any drug that harms your driving can bring the same penalties as drunk driving. Adults over 21 may legally have marijuana. But driving high is still illegal.
items.official: If your driving is impaired because you are under the influence of any drug, you may face the same penalties as driving under the influence of alcohol. Although the possession of marijuana and marijuana products (over the age of 21) is legal, driving under the influence of marijuana is still illegal. Smoking or consuming cannabis will affect how you drive.
items.mnemonic: Legal to have is not legal to drive.

items.title: Implied consent: breath test
items.simple: If you drive on Virginia's public roads, you agree to take a breath test if police ask. This is implied consent. Police with probable cause can arrest you for DUI within 3 hours after a crash, without a warrant.
items.official: If the police have probable cause to stop you and suspect that you have been drinking or using drugs, they will ask you to take a breath or blood test. Under implied consent laws, if you operate a motor vehicle on Virginia's public roads, you agree to take a breath test upon request. If you are involved in a motor vehicle crash and a law enforcement officer has probable cause, you can be arrested for DUI within three hours of the crash without a warrant and at any location.
items.mnemonic: Drive here, agree to blow. After a crash: 3 hours, no warrant.

items.title: Automatic suspension: 7 days first
items.simple: Refusing a breath test or being charged with DUI at .08 or more suspends your license automatically. It lasts 7 days for a first offense, 60 days or until trial for a second, and until trial for a third.
items.official: If you refuse a breath test or your BAC is .08 percent or higher while you are driving and law enforcement charges you with DUI, your driving privilege will be automatically suspended: for seven days, for a first offense; for 60 days or until you go to trial, whichever comes first, for a second offense; until the trial, for a third DUI offense. If you are convicted of DUI, the court and DMV will impose a suspension/revocation and other penalties in addition to the administrative license suspension. If you receive multiple DUI convictions, the suspension/revocation periods will run consecutively.
items.mnemonic: 7 days, then 60, then trial.

items.title: Open container: passenger area
items.simple: Police can charge you with drinking while driving if they stop you, find an open, partly empty alcohol container in the passenger area, and see signs of drinking. An unlocked glove box is part of the passenger area.
items.official: You may be charged with drinking while operating a motor vehicle if you are stopped by law enforcement and you have an open container of alcohol in the passenger area and the contents have been partially removed, and show signs that you have been drinking. The passenger area means the area that seats the driver and passengers and any area within the driver's reach, including an unlocked glove compartment.
items.mnemonic: If the driver can reach it, it counts. Even an unlocked glove box.

items.title: DUI with a child: extra penalty
items.simple: You must spend 5 extra days in jail for a DUI with a child (age 17 or younger) in the car. You may also pay an extra $500 to $1,000. A second offense adds 80 hours of community service.
items.official: Conviction of any DUI offense involving a juvenile passenger (age 17 or younger) in the vehicle at the time of the offense carries an additional mandatory five-day jail term plus all other fines and jail sentences. You may also be charged an additional fine of at least $500 and up to $1,000. A second DUI offense with a juvenile in the vehicle carries an additional 80-hour community service requirement.
items.mnemonic: Kid in the car: plus 5 days jail, plus $500 to $1,000.

items.title: Car impounded 30 days
items.simple: If you drive after your license is suspended for an alcohol offense, your car is taken away (impounded) right away for 30 days. If you are convicted, the court can keep it for 90 more days.
items.official: Your vehicle will be impounded immediately for 30 days if you are caught driving after your license has been suspended for an alcohol-related offense. The court can impound the vehicle for an additional 90 days if you are convicted. If you drive without a license after a previous conviction for driving without a license, the vehicle is impounded until you obtain a license or for three days, whichever is less.
items.mnemonic: 30 now, 90 more if convicted.

items.title: DUI crash: pay up to $1,000
items.simple: If your DUI causes a crash, you may have to pay for the police, EMS, firefighters and rescue workers who respond. It can cost up to $1,000. This depends on the laws of the city or county.
items.official: Depending on the laws of the city or county in which you are driving, you may be responsible for paying the cost (up to $1,000) for law enforcement, emergency medical services, fire fighters and rescue personnel who respond to a crash or incident resulting from your DUI violation.

items.title: Under 21: lose license 1 year
items.simple: Under 21, you cannot buy, have or drink alcohol. A conviction for driving with a BAC of .02 to under .08 suspends your license for 1 year. You also pay at least $500 or do 50 hours of community service.
items.official: If you are under age 21, you cannot purchase, possess or consume alcohol. If you are convicted of driving after illegally consuming alcohol, and your BAC was at least .02 percent and less than .08 percent, the court penalty will include a suspension of your driving privilege for one year from the date of conviction, and a minimum mandatory fine of $500, or the requirement that you complete at least 50 hours of community service. Virginia has a zero tolerance law against underage drinking. If you are convicted of driving after illegally consuming alcohol and your BAC was .08 percent or higher, you may face the same penalties as an adult.
items.mnemonic: Zero tolerance: 1 year off the road, plus $500 OR 50 hours.

items.title: Giving alcohol to under 21
items.simple: Never give or sell alcohol to anyone under 21, anyone drunk or anyone a court told not to drink. You can be fined up to $2,500, jailed for 12 months and lose your license for up to 1 year.
items.official: If you provide or sell alcoholic beverages to a person under age 21 or someone who is intoxicated or ordered by a court to refrain from drinking alcohol, you are subject to a fine up to $2,500, mandatory suspension of your driver's license for up to one year, and 12 months in jail.

items.title: Fake ID: big penalties
items.simple: Under 21, using a fake ID to get alcohol means a fine of at least $500, at least 50 hours of community service and up to 12 months in jail. Your license is suspended for 6 months to 1 year.
items.official: If you are under age 21 and you use or attempt to use a fake ID to establish a false age in an attempt to drink or purchase alcohol, you will: be fined at least $500; be required to perform at least 50 hours of community service; face up to 12 months in jail; and face mandatory suspension of your driver's license for at least six months but not more than one year.
items.mnemonic: Fake ID: $500 AND 50 hours. (Under-21 drinking is $500 OR 50 hours.)
